exploratory_probes.note: 'bend test' occurs verbatim in THREE documents: ferment_005, ferment_006 (both fermentation cards) and recipe_169 (a distractor card's Tips section: 'The bend test on the cabbage stem is the correct measure of salting, not the timer.'). No single recipe_id is 'the' right answer here - this probe exists to show what hybrid actually does to a real rare-term collision, not to be scored pass/fail.

Recipe: Traditional Napa Cabbage Kimchi (recipe_id: ferment_005)
Section: Method

Quarter the cabbage lengthwise keeping the core attached, then brine it using the full 160 g of coarse sea salt, working the salt between the leaves and concentrating it on the thick white stems. Leave for 4 to 6 hours, turning every 2 hours.

The cabbage is correctly brined when a thick white stem bends into a U shape without snapping. This bend test matters more than the clock, because cabbage size and moisture content vary considerably between heads.

Rinse three times in cold water and drain cut side down for at least one hour. Residual water dilutes the paste and can spoil the ferment.

Recipe: Napa Cabbage Kimchi (recipe_id: recipe_169)
Section: Tips

- The bend test on the cabbage stem is the correct measure of salting, not the timer.
- Drain the cabbage thoroughly after rinsing.
- Press out all air pockets and keep the cabbage submerged under its brine.
- Open the container once a day during the room-temperature stage to release built-up gas.

Recipe: Vegan Napa Cabbage Kimchi (recipe_id: ferment_006)
Section: Method

Brine the quartered cabbage with the full 160 g of coarse sea salt for 4 to 6 hours, turning every 2 hours, then apply the bend test: a thick white stem should bend into a U without snapping. Rinse three times and drain cut side down for one hour.

Build the umami base while the cabbage brines. Simmer the dried shiitake and the kombu in 400 ml of water for 20 minutes, then remove the kombu before it turns slimy and simmer the shiitake for a further 10 minutes. Strain, reserving 250 ml of the liquid, and finely chop the rehydrated shiitake caps to fold into the paste.

Recipe: Sourdough Brioche (recipe_id: ferment_004)
Section: Method

Mix the flour, cold milk, eggs, sugar and levain in a stand mixer with the dough hook on low for 4 minutes until a shaggy dough forms. Add the fine sea salt and mix on medium for a further 8 minutes until the dough is smooth and pulls cleanly from the sides of the bowl.

Only now begin adding the softened butter, roughly 50 g at a time, waiting until each addition has fully disappeared before adding the next. The butter goes in last and gradually, because adding it at the start coats the flour in fat and prevents the gluten network from developing at all. Expect this stage to take 10 to 12 minutes.

The dough is ready when it passes the windowpane test: a small piece stretched thin should become translucent without tearing.

Recipe: Aloo Paratha (recipe_id: recipe_040)
Section: Tips

- The filling must be dry; if it feels wet, add a tablespoon of roasted besan or leave the onion out entirely.
- Refrigerating boiled potatoes before mashing makes the filling much easier to handle.
- Roll gently and evenly rather than pressing hard in one place, which is what causes tears.
- Cook on medium heat, since high heat browns the surface before the dough cooks through.

Recipe: Plain Dosa (recipe_id: recipe_002)
Section: Instructions

1. Take the fermented batter out of the refrigerator 30 minutes before cooking so it comes to room temperature. Cold batter sticks to the pan.
2. Stir the batter gently with a ladle. Do not beat it hard or you will knock out the air from fermentation. Add water a tablespoon at a time until the batter is pourable and coats the back of a spoon thinly.
3. Heat a flat cast iron tawa or heavy non-stick griddle over medium-high heat for 3 to 4 minutes. Test it by flicking a few drops of water onto the surface: they should dance and evaporate within 2 seconds.
4. Dip the cut face of the halved onion into oil and rub it across the hot griddle. This seasons the surface and prevents sticking.
5. Reduce the heat to medium. Pour a full ladle of batter into the centre of the tawa.
6. Using the back of the ladle, spread the batter outward in a continuous spiral from the centre to the edge, working quickly, until you have a thin circle about 25cm across. Do not go back over an area you have already spread.
7. Drizzle 1 teaspoon of oil around the outer edge and a few drops in the centre.
8. Cook undisturbed for 2 to 3 minutes on medium-high heat. The dosa is ready when the base is evenly golden brown, the surface looks dry, and the edges curl away from the griddle on their own.
9. Fold the dosa in half or roll it into a cylinder with a spatula and lift it off. There is no need to cook the second side for a crisp dosa.
10. Before making the next dosa, wipe the griddle with a damp cloth held in tongs and let it cool slightly. Repeat until the batter is used up.

Recipe: Rye Levain Starter (recipe_id: ferment_002)
Section: Method

Cover loosely and ferment for 8 to 12 hours at 22 to 24C. The levain is ripe when it has at least doubled from the elastic band mark, the surface is domed and covered in fine bubbles, and it smells sharply sour with a faint acetone note. A levain that has risen and then collapsed back to a flat, watery surface has gone past ripe and will give a slack, over-acidified dough.

The float test is a useful confirmation: drop a teaspoon of ripe levain into room temperature water and it should float rather than sink.

Refresh at least once every 24 hours if the starter is kept at room temperature, or once a week if it is stored at 4C in the refrigerator.
